chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order. Dot plots turn the mean into a balance point, and every change to the data (a new value, a missing value, every value shifted or doubled) is predicted first and then checked. The second half moves from numbers to pictures: line graphs, an infographic and colour strips, each read with the same two questions, what is given and what does it say.

points.title: Predict, then check
points.text: Each idea opens with a question the student answers before the video reveals it: will the mean go up or down, which dot is missing, which season is wet. The tool then lets the student test the guess.

points.title: One tool, one idea
points.text: Every topic has one tool, and no tool is used twice. A tool appears only where handling the data is the concept itself.

points.title: Read a graph in two steps
points.text: Step one: what is given (axes, scale, marks, who collected it and how). Step two: what can be inferred, and what cannot. Graph values are read approximately and said so.

points.title: Ask your own questions
points.text: The chapter closes on projects: strips of the student's own day, sleep logs and school timings, because looking at data leads to new questions.

concepts.concept_name: The mean of two numbers sits halfway

content.text:
5.1 The Balancing Act
Last year, we learnt about the mean and median. Recall that the mean of some data is the sum of all the values divided by the number of values in the data. The median is the middle value when the data is sorted.
We shall try to understand the mean and median from a different perspective and see how the mean behaves with changing data.
Consider any 2 numbers. Find their average/arithmetic mean. Repeat this by taking other pairs. What do you observe?
For example, let the two numbers be 3 and 7. Their average is (3 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5. Taking another pair of numbers, say 8 and 9, their average is (8 + 9) ÷ 2 = 8.5. Visualising these as dot plots we get the picture. Notice that the mean is exactly halfway between the two numbers.

concepts.concept_name: The mean as the balance point

content.text:
Calculate and mark the mean of each collection of data below.
Can you explain how the mean is the centre of each collection?
Is the mean the midpoint of the two endpoints/extremes of the data? It is not always so. Instead, the total distances are equal on both the sides of the mean.
Verify that this holds for all the collections of data shown earlier.
Can there be more than one such centre? In other words, is there any other value such that the sum of the distances to the values lower than it and the values higher than it will still be equal?
In the case of the collection 10, 10, 11, and 17 whose mean is 12, suppose there is a different centre larger than 12. Clearly, all the distances on the LHS will increase and the distances on the RHS will decrease. Thus, it is no longer the centre. Similarly, for any value smaller than 12, the distances on the LHS will decrease while those on the RHS will increase.
Therefore, there is only one centre.

1. Predict first: for 10, 10, 11 and 17, is the mean the midpoint of 10 and 17? Check it before reading on.
2. The mean is 12, but the midpoint of 10 and 17 is 13.5. So the mean is not the midpoint of the extremes. What it balances is distance.
3. Distances to the left of 12 add to 2 + 2 + 1 = 5. The distance to the right is 17 − 12 = 5. Equal.
4. Move the finger to 13: the left distances grow, the right distance shrinks, no balance. Move to 11: the opposite. Only 12 balances, so there is only one centre.

Worked example: Show that the mean of 10, 10, 11 and 17 balances the distances, and that 13 does not.
1. The mean is (10 + 10 + 11 + 17) ÷ 4 = 48 ÷ 4 = 12.
2. Left of 12: 2 + 2 + 1 = 5. Right of 12: 17 − 12 = 5. They are equal.

4. Try 11. Left of 11: 1 + 1 + 0 = 2. Right of 11: 6 + 0 = 6. Not equal.
Answer: Only 12 balances the distances; 13 and 11 do not

concepts.concept_name: A value added, removed or kept: the mean moves

content.text:
Will including a new value in the data increase or decrease the mean?
When a new value greater than the mean is included, the mean increases to maintain the balance between the sum of distances on the LHS and RHS. Similarly, if a value smaller than the mean is included, then the new mean will be less than before.
What happens to the mean when an existing value is removed? When will the mean increase, decrease, or stay the same? What happens to the mean if a value equal to the mean is included or removed? Try to explain this using the fair-share interpretation of mean that we studied last year.
Unchanging Mean! Explore if it is possible to include or remove 2 values such that the mean is unchanged.
How about including or removing 3 values without changing the mean? Is it possible? Can we include 2 values less than the mean and 1 value greater than the mean, so that the mean remains the same?
Try to include 2 values greater than the mean and 1 value less than the mean, so that the mean stays the same.

concepts.concept_name: Every value shifted or multiplied

content.text:
What happens to the mean if every value in the collection increases by some fixed number?

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students mark the mean of a dot plot, verify that the total distance to values on the left equals the total on the right, and explain why a second centre cannot exist.
Students find the mean of a second collection that is not a whole number and check that the distances to the values on its left and right still add to the same total.
Students predict whether the mean rises, falls or stays when one value is added or removed, and find pairs or triples of values that leave the mean unchanged.
Students choose two values, one below and one above the mean by the same amount, include them in the data, and check that the mean stays exactly the same.
Students predict and prove that adding a fixed number to every value adds it to the mean, subtracting subtracts it, and multiplying every value multiplies the mean by that number.
Students write the sum of n values with mean a, subtract 2 from each value, and show with algebra that the new mean is exactly a minus 2.
Students drag dots, add and remove values, and shift or scale the whole data on a dot plot, predicting each time where the mean will land and checking the balance of distances.

concepts.concept_name: Tinkering with the median

content.text:
We know that the median is the middle value in the sorted data: there are an equal number of values less than it and greater than it.
Will including a new value to the data increase or decrease the median? Let us consider the following data. The median of this data is 8.
Suppose we include a value 11. The new value included is greater than the (earlier) median: the median can no longer be 8 as there are more values greater than it. Therefore, the median will also increase. The median, now, will be the average of the two middle values 8 and 11, which is 9.5.
We can similarly argue that when a value less than the median is included, the median will decrease.

Worked example: A data set has median 8 and its two middle values after including 11 are 8 and 11. Find the new median.

3. 9.5 is above 8, so the median rose, as predicted.

concepts.concept_name: Finding the unknown: a missing weight

content.text:
Coach Balwan noted down the weights of the kushti players (wrestlers) and the mean as shown. But one value that was written down got smudged. Can you find out the missing value?
Average weight of the players = Sum of weight of all players ÷ Number of players.
Let the unknown weight be w kg. (42 + 40 + 39 + 33 + 48 + 38 + 42 + 35 + 32 + w) ÷ 10 = 39.2. Simplifying this we get, 349 + w = 392, w = 392 − 349 = 43. The missing value is 43 kg.

concepts.concept_name: Finding the unknown: a harvest corrected

content.text:
Venkayya keeps track of the coconut harvest in his farm. He calculates the average harvest per tree as 25.6. His son verifies the counts and finds that one tree's harvest count is incorrectly noted as 3 more than the actual number. Can you find the correct average if the number of trees is 15?
The data of harvest per tree is not given. Can we still find out the number of coconuts harvested?
z ÷ 15 = 25.6, so z = 25.6 × 15 = 384. The actual total harvest count is 384 − 3 = 381. The correct average harvest is 381 ÷ 15 = 25.4.

Figure it Out (mean and median, question 6): Justify whether each statement is always true, sometimes true or never true: (i) Removing a value less than the median will decrease the median. (ii) Including a value less than the mean will decrease the mean. (iii) Including any 4 values will not affect the median. (iv) Including 4 values less than the median will increase the median.
1. (i) Never true. The middle moves up or stays; for 1, 2, 3 removing 1 gives 2 and 3 with median 2.5.
2. (ii) Always true. A value below the mean adds more left distance, so the balance point moves down.
3. (iii) Sometimes true. Two low and two high values leave it; four high values do not.
4. (iv) Never true. Values below the median push it down or leave it.
Answer: (i) never (ii) always (iii) sometimes (iv) never

Figure it Out (mean and median, question 9): Consider the data 12, 47, 8, 73, 18, 35, 39, 8, 29, 25, p. Which of these could be p if the median is 29? (i) 10 (ii) 25 (iii) 40 (iv) 100 (v) 29 (vi) 47 (vii) 30

2. Without p the sorted values are 8, 8, 12, 18, 25, 29, 35, 39, 47, 73.

Answer: p could be 40, 100, 29, 47 or 30, that is (iii), (iv), (v), (vi), (vii)

Figure it Out (more on mean and median, question 6): Two new students join a class whose average height was 150.2 cm with 24 students. (i) Which statements are correct? (ii) The new heights are 149 cm and 152 cm: what happens to the mean? (iii) What happens to the median?
1. (i) The new heights have to be measured, since they decide the new average. The others claim too much.
2. (ii) 149 is 1.2 below 150.2 and 152 is 1.8 above. The surplus wins, so the average increases slightly: (24 × 150.2 + 149 + 152) ÷ 26 ≈ 150.22.
3. (iii) The median depends on the actual heights, which we are not given, so there is not enough information.
Answer: (i) the new heights must be measured (ii) the average increases (iii) not enough information

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students predict the direction in which the median moves when a value above or below it is included or removed, and compute the new median as the average of two middle values.
Students write an equation from a given mean, a given count and one smudged value, and solve it to find the missing value.
Students recover a total from a mean and a count, correct the total for an error in one value, and find the corrected mean without the individual data.
Students use a given mean or median with a count to build an equation, find the missing value or the corrected result, and test claims about adding or removing values.

media.description: Four statements about removing or including values are tested on small lists. Each is judged to be always true, sometimes true or never true, with a reason from where the middle value or the balance point moves.

maths_rules: (i) 1, 2, 3 has median 2; removing 1 leaves 2, 3 with median 2.5; removing a value below the median moves the median up or leaves it, so never true
(ii) 4, 6 has mean 5; including 2 gives total 12 over 3 values, mean 4; a value below the mean always lowers the mean, so always true
(iii) 1, 2, 3 plus 0, 0, 10, 10 sorted is 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 10, 10 with median 2 (unchanged); 1, 2, 3 plus 10, 10, 10, 10 sorted is 1, 2, 3, 10, 10, 10, 10 with median 10 (changed); so sometimes true
(iv) 1, 2, 3 plus four 0s sorted is 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3 with median 0 (lower, not higher); values below the median never raise it, so never true
check: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 has median 3; plus four 0s sorted is 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and the 5th value is 1, so the median fell from 3 to 1

media.title: Which values can the missing eleventh value be?
media.context: Tales by Dots and Lines. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Ten values are known and an eleventh value p is missing. The median of all eleven must be twenty nine, which is the sixth value when sorted. Testing where p lands in the sorted list shows which of the seven choices work.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the median of eleven values is the sixth sorted value, so a missing value must not push the known twenty nine out of sixth place. Watch for students who test only the choices one at a time without sorting.

maths_rules: with p there are 11 values, so the median is the 6th sorted value
if p is at least 29, the six smallest values are 8, 8, 12, 18, 25, 29, so the 6th is 29
if p is less than 29, the six smallest values include p and the 6th is less than 29 (25 when p is at most 25, and p when p is between 25 and 29)
10 and 25 are less than 29, so they fail; 40, 100, 29, 47 and 30 are at least 29, so they work
